progress: Regressed, the roadmap stands and its own delivery reporting withdrew a quantified claim
summary: The Cabinet-adopted roadmap is unchanged, but Operation Vulindlela's reporting moved from [80% of initiatives on track](2026-04-23-operation-vulindlela-digital-transformation) to [uneven and slower than anticipated](2026-07-31-sa-operation-vulindlela-q1-2026-progress-report).
developments:
The instrument itself did not move. The Digital Transformation of Government Roadmap was [approved by Cabinet in March 2025](2025-03-27-cabinet-statement-26-march-2025), before this window opened, and nothing in the twelve months amends, replaces or reviews it.

What moved is the account of its delivery. A briefing in April 2026 [put 80% of digital transformation initiatives on track](2026-04-23-operation-vulindlela-digital-transformation) with a fifth complete. The quarterly report of July 2026 [replaces that with a statement that progress has been uneven and in certain instances slower than initially anticipated](2026-07-31-sa-operation-vulindlela-q1-2026-progress-report), and publishes no later percentage. A quantified claim withdrawn and not restated is a worse position than the one it replaced, whatever the underlying delivery did.

Cabinet's own diagnosis of the problem — interdepartmental coordination, outdated systems, overlapping mandates and limited skills — names institutional fragmentation rather than technology.

progress: Advanced, a tender for a modelling system rather than a strategy
summary: The communications department [tendered on 11 August 2026 for an ICT indicators and scenario-modelling system to steer the digital economy to 2050](2026-08-11-sa-dcdt-2050-digital-economy-vision-tender); nothing is awarded or built.
developments:
2026-08-11 — the department [put out to tender a system of ICT indicators and scenario modelling running to 2050](2026-08-11-sa-dcdt-2050-digital-economy-vision-tender), framed against the National Digital Transformation Roadmap, the Presidential Commission on the Fourth Industrial Revolution and the Digital Economy Masterplan.

What is tendered is the instrumentation, not the strategy: no award, value or delivery date is published, and the three documents it is framed against are the standing position it would measure. A second monitoring instrument appeared in the same month — the Presidency and the planning department [went to the parliamentary committee to fast-track a digital dashboard for mega infrastructure projects](2026-08-13-parliament-sona-digital-dashboard-committee-presidency), again with no delivery date, data source or custodian named, and no statement of whether it will be public.

progress: Mixed, a cost study and a spectrum roadmap advanced while the release they depend on stayed unscheduled
summary: The department [tendered a market study toward a Cost to Communicate Roadmap](2026-08-01-sas-data-price-puzzle) and the regulator [consulted an IMT roadmap to 2030](2026-07-28-icasa-imt-roadmap-2026-6g-spectrum-consultation), but [no auction is scheduled, priced or gazetted](2026-08-03-sa-icasa-nrfp-spectrum-eussc-mtn-vodacom-legal-challenge).
developments:
2026-08-01 — the department [put a market analysis study out to tender](2026-08-01-sas-data-price-puzzle), conceding in the tender document a current policy vacuum and that the price benefits expected from the 2022 spectrum auction remain largely unmet. It names market concentration, spectrum allocation and the burden on prepaid consumers as the structural causes, and asks for a roadmap of short-, medium- and long-term reforms plus an assessment of the regulator's measures.

2026-07-24 — the regulator [gazetted an IMT Roadmap to 2026 with draft assignment plans](2026-07-24-imt-roadmap-2026-gazette-55068) and [opened consultation reaching to IMT-2030](2026-07-28-icasa-imt-roadmap-2026-6g-spectrum-consultation). The roadmap [records 794 MHz assigned against 19,625 MHz identified](2026-07-24-imt-roadmap-2026-gazette-55068).

Against both, the release itself has not moved: the 2026 frequency plan [targets 1,145 MHz more mid-band spectrum and over 17,250 MHz of mmWave, but no auction has been scheduled, priced or gazetted](2026-08-03-sa-icasa-nrfp-spectrum-eussc-mtn-vodacom-legal-challenge). A study of why prices are high and a roadmap of what could be assigned are both downstream of an auction nobody has dated.

summary: The National Policy on Data and Cloud [was gazetted as final in May 2024](2024-05-31-national-policy-on-data-and-cloud), settling a question this report had carried as an open draft.
developments:
[The policy was gazetted as final](2024-05-31-national-policy-on-data-and-cloud). That corrects the position this report previously carried, which was that the instrument remained a draft unresolved since 2021 — a reading drawn from [a research account that describes it as a draft](2025-01-01 South African Digital Sovereignty at the Crossroad of Securitization and Development (Chapter 4) - Digital Sovereignty in the BRICS Countries).

What the policy does is not small: it declares that data generated in the country shall be the property of the country and provides for in-country copies for law enforcement, which sits markedly apart from the adequacy logic the data protection Act runs on.

2025-12-11 — [a policy direction now requires the communications regulator to weigh data sovereignty, data protection and data security in sector ownership regulation](2025-12-11-policy-direction-icasa-bbbee-data-sovereignty), which is the first time the policy reaches into licensing.

summary: The national data exchange pilot [has infrastructure operational and four departments testing it](2026-01-01-operation-vulindlela-phase-ii-progress-report-q3-2025-26), on a term ending in September 2026.
developments:
[A one-year pilot runs from October 2025 to September 2026 with four task teams, interoperability standards and draft data-exchange legislation as its deliverables](2025-09-27-mzansixchange-pilot-programme).

2026-01 — [pilot infrastructure is operational at the national research council, with home affairs, the social security agency, the student aid scheme and the public service department testing it and a working single-citizen application prototype built](2026-01-01-operation-vulindlela-phase-ii-progress-report-q3-2025-26). 2026-06-23 — [the pilot is confirmed as ending in September 2026](2026-06-23-parliament-atc-109-2026).

So the roadmap exists as a dated pilot with named participants and named deliverables, which is more than most instruments on this ledger carry. What it does not carry is a decision point: no source states what happens at the end of September, or who decides.

summary: The draft national AI policy was [withdrawn in April 2026 over fabricated academic citations](2026-04-28-ai-hallucination-policy-withdrawal), the [seven institutions it proposed are under reconsideration](2026-07-31-sa-parliament-against-new-ai-watchdogs-diko), and [cabinet has slipped to November 2026 or January 2027](2026-05-27-sa-delays-ai-policy-2027).
developments:
2026-04 — the draft national policy, released for comment on 10 April 2026, was [withdrawn after AI-hallucinated citations were found in its reference list](2026-04-28-ai-hallucination-policy-withdrawal). Two officials were on precautionary suspension [as at 19 August 2026](2026-08-19-citizen-activate-sa-ai-policy-summit).

2026-05-12 — [an expert panel was appointed](2026-05-12-malatsi-ai-expert-panel) to advise the redraft.

2026-07-29 — the department stated the replacement [will issue national guidelines rather than prescribe rules to industry](2026-07-29-south-africa-national-ai-policy-radical-rethink), and that the seven proposed new institutions are being reconsidered. Parliament's communications committee [prefers strengthening the existing regulators through the ICT and Media Regulators Forum](2026-07-31-sa-parliament-against-new-ai-watchdogs-diko) to creating them.

2026-05-27 — [cabinet consideration moved to November 2026 with January 2027 as the fallback](2026-05-27-sa-delays-ai-policy-2027). South Africa has no gazetted national AI policy framework, and the instrument that was in the window went backwards rather than forwards.

summary: The only localisation instrument is the same [unresolved draft data and cloud policy](2025-01-01 South African Digital Sovereignty at the Crossroad of Securitization and Development (Chapter 4) - Digital Sovereignty in the BRICS Countries), which would vest data generated in South Africa in the state.
developments:
Localisation in South Africa rests on a draft. The [draft data and cloud policy declares that data generated in South Africa shall be the property of South Africa and provides for in-country copies for law enforcement](2025-01-01 South African Digital Sovereignty at the Crossroad of Securitization and Development (Chapter 4) - Digital Sovereignty in the BRICS Countries); it has not been gazetted and nothing in the window moved it.

What is in force runs the other way. The data protection Act operates an adequacy model — [cross-border transfers are permitted where equivalent protection, consent or contractual necessity applies](2026-07-06-popia-five-years-nobody-accountable), with the responsible party accountable — so the position a reader would take from the statute and the position the draft policy would create are not the same, and the base holds no decision reconciling them.

summary: The National Policy on Data and Cloud [was gazetted in May 2024](2024-05-31-national-policy-on-data-and-cloud), and [a policy direction of December 2025 pushes data sovereignty into sector ownership regulation](2025-12-11-policy-direction-icasa-bbbee-data-sovereignty).
developments:
[The policy was gazetted as final in May 2024](2024-05-31-national-policy-on-data-and-cloud), which settles a question this report had carried open: the instrument is made, not still in draft.

2025-12-11 — [a formal policy direction requires the communications regulator to weigh data sovereignty, data protection and data security in sector ownership regulation](2025-12-11-policy-direction-icasa-bbbee-data-sovereignty). That is the policy reaching into licensing, and it is the first instrument on this ledger to do so.

What is still missing is implementation: no data classification standard, no public-sector data catalogue and no reporting against the policy appears, and the localisation duty it contemplates is reported separately under data localisation.

summary: A [National Open Science Policy is on the books with no commencement date stated](2026-03-01-south-african-open-science-policy); no open data policy of general application is held.
developments:
The base holds one instrument in this space, a [National Open Science Policy](2026-03-01-south-african-open-science-policy), and records that no commencement date is stated for it. Nothing in the twelve months to 2026-08-26 commences, amends or reports against it.

It is also narrower than the indicator: an open science policy governs publicly funded research output, not government administrative data. No open data policy of general application, no national portal and no publication duty on departments appears anywhere on this ledger.

progress: No change, amendment work on AI and privacy by design is stated and nothing is enacted
summary: The Act is unamended. The regulator [told a webinar on 18 August 2026 it is working with the justice department to amend it to cover artificial intelligence and privacy by design](2026-08-18-timeslive-sahrc-personal-information-digital-age).
developments:
The statute did not move in the window. What is on the record is an intention: the regulator [stated on 18 August 2026 that it is working with the justice department to amend the Act to cover artificial intelligence and privacy by design](2026-08-18-timeslive-sahrc-personal-information-digital-age), and in the same session that it has no capability to test external systems for privacy compliance before launch.

The Act's own terms are unchanged and its ceiling is low against the harm it addresses: [five years on, the maximum fine remains R10m](2026-07-06-popia-five-years-nobody-accountable) against an average measured breach cost several times that. No amendment Bill, gazette notice or draft text is held, so this is a stated programme of work rather than a legislative step.

summary: The Cybercrimes Act [is in force](2021-06-01-cybercrimes-act-19-of-2020), the state [signed the United Nations cybercrime convention in October 2025](2025-10-30-minister-kubayi-remarks-g20-acwg-ministerial-meeting), and [a revised strategy awaits adoption](2026-05-22-state-security-agency-budget-vote-2026-27-cybersecurity-strategy).
developments:
[The Cybercrimes Act is the standing substantive statute](2021-06-01-cybercrimes-act-19-of-2020), held as an excerpt.

2025-10-25 — [the state signed the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime](2025-10-30-minister-kubayi-remarks-g20-acwg-ministerial-meeting), told to a G20 ministerial by the justice minister. No ratification step has followed.

2026-05-22 — [consultation on a revised National Cybersecurity Strategy is substantially complete with adoption expected in the following quarter](2026-05-22-state-security-agency-budget-vote-2026-27-cybersecurity-strategy). No adopted text is on file, so the strategy is an expectation stated in a budget vote.

Signature, a statute and a strategy in consultation is a fuller legislative position than most countries in this base hold, and none of the three is a report of enforcement: no prosecution count under the Act appears anywhere on this ledger.

progress: Advanced, the regulations moved ahead of the Bill they are said to rest on
summary: Draft identification regulations were [gazetted on 4 May 2026](2026-05-06-digital-id-draft-regulation-gazetted) and consulted to 6 June, while the [National Identification and Registration Bill is still before Parliament](2026-05-29 Opinion South Africa's Digital Identity Regulations A Governance Crossroads).
developments:
2026-05-04 — draft amendments to the Identification Regulations were [gazetted](2026-05-06-digital-id-draft-regulation-gazetted), with a 33-day comment period closing on 6 June 2026. They would create [voluntary digital-ID credentials with legal parity to the physical document](2026-05-09-smart-ids-go-digital-draft-rules), grant accredited trusted entities API access to the population register under data-sharing agreements, and set three assurance levels, seven-year audit logs and private-sector enrolment points, with finalisation dated September 2026.

The primary legislation has not kept pace. The [National Identification and Registration Bill remains before Parliament](2026-05-29 Opinion South Africa's Digital Identity Regulations A Governance Crossroads), named as the statutory foundation the regulations should rest on, and the record does not say whether its passage is now a precondition. A submission on the closing day asked the department to suspend the regulations pending that Bill, a published digital identity policy and demonstrated compliance with the data protection Act, on the ground that a biometric enrolment and real-time verification system is being built with no formal role for the Information Regulator. That submission is held as a supplied document with no published address, so it cannot be linked here.

summary: A National Payment System Bill will go out for public comment, moving payment regulation from entity-based to activity-based ([announcement](2026-09-01-national-payment-system-bill-techcentral)).
developments:
The Reserve Bank governor said on 1 September 2026 that the National Payment System Bill will soon go out for public comment, moving payment regulation from an entity-based model to an activity-based one ([announcement](2026-09-01-national-payment-system-bill-techcentral)).

An activity-based model is what would open payment licensing to non-banks, which the base currently carries as a not-held position.

Nothing is enacted: the base holds a governor's statement of intent, no published bill text, no comment period dates and no commencement provision.

summary: Draft data-exchange legislation [is a stated deliverable of the exchange pilot](2025-09-27-mzansixchange-pilot-programme), over [a 2014 statute that already provides for administration-wide norms and standards](2014-12-22-public-administration-management-act-11-of-2014).
developments:
The standing instrument is not a data law. [The Public Administration Management Act has been in force since 2014 as the frame for administration-wide arrangements across national, provincial and municipal spheres, including the transfer and secondment of employees and the establishment of common norms and standards](2014-12-22-public-administration-management-act-11-of-2014) — which is the authority under which service standards are set, and it says nothing about data.

[Draft data-exchange legislation is one of three named deliverables of the one-year exchange pilot](2025-09-27-mzansixchange-pilot-programme), alongside four task teams and interoperability standards.

So the country is running a federated data exchange in pilot with no statute behind it, and the statute is scheduled to be drafted by the pilot itself. Nothing on this ledger states who would introduce it or when.

summary: [No rules govern state automated decision-making](2026-07-22-ai-hallucinations-strike-again-at-sa-courts). What moved instead was [litigation over an algorithmic grant eligibility screen](2026-08-13-sassa-algorithm-social-grants-amicus-gcg) and a copyright Bill silent on AI.
developments:
The position is unchanged and stated as such: the base holds [no instrument governing automated decision-making by the state](2026-07-22-ai-hallucinations-strike-again-at-sa-courts).

What the window produced is a court case rather than a rule. The state is [appealing a January 2025 judgment that struck down regulations governing the Social Relief of Distress grant](2026-08-13-sassa-algorithm-social-grants-amicus-gcg), a scheme administered online only and screened by an algorithmic verification system that excluded applicants it read as earning above R624.00; the court found the automation unfairly excluded otherwise eligible applicants, an AI governance organisation was admitted as a friend of the court, and the appeal was set down for 25 August 2026.

The one Bill in the window that touches machine learning does so silently. The [Copyright Amendment Bill would replace fair dealing with a broader fair use exception](2026-07-31-anthropic-book-scanning-south-african-authors) and returned to Parliament in June 2026 after the Constitutional Court upheld most of it; it says nothing explicit about generative AI or text and data mining, which imports another country's judicial answer to those questions along with the doctrine.

summary: The 2002 electronic transactions statute [is the standing law](2002-08-02-electronic-communications-and-transactions-act-25-of-2002), [platform competition guidance was gazetted in February 2026](2026-02-06-final-online-intermediation-platforms-guidance-note), and [a market inquiry imposed binding remedies on six platform companies](2025-11-13-compcom-mdpmi-final-report).
developments:
[The Electronic Communications and Transactions Act has been in force since 2002 as the legal basis for electronic contracting and data messages](2002-08-02-electronic-communications-and-transactions-act-25-of-2002), held as an excerpt, with no amendment or successor bill on file.

2025-11-13 — [the competition authority's media and digital platforms market inquiry closed with binding remedial actions under section 43D(1) for Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok and X, on a finding that 77% of the population take social media as their main online source of news](2025-11-13-compcom-mdpmi-final-report). [Google's remedies commit up to ZAR 687,500,000 over their five-year term](2025-11-13-compcom-mdpmi-final-report-annexure8-remedial-actions).

2026-02-06 — [final guidance for leading online intermediation platforms was gazetted, naming price-parity clauses, interoperability restrictions, self-preferencing and misuse of competitively sensitive data as the competition risks the commission will act on](2026-02-06-final-online-intermediation-platforms-guidance-note). It is guidance rather than regulation and no enforcement action under it is on file.

Beyond the inquiry's remedies, the enforcement on file is a municipal one: three online grocery platforms had premises closed in a health and licensing operation, reported under local government.

summary: The Statistics Amendment Act [has been proclaimed for implementation](2026-03-11-stats-sa-2025-26-q3-report-portfolio-committee), with [regulations and twenty memoranda of understanding under development](2026-06-23-parliament-atc-109-2026) to carry it.
developments:
[The Statistics Act of 1999 is the standing statute](1999-04-21-statistics-act-6-of-1999-2) and [the Amendment Act was assented in December 2024](2024-12-20-statistics-amendment-act-29-of-2024).

2026-03-11 — [the Amendment Act had been proclaimed for implementation and implementation was reported as progressing](2026-03-11-stats-sa-2025-26-q3-report-portfolio-committee); the proclamation date itself is not stated in the held account.

2026-06-23 — [regulations and twenty memoranda of understanding are under development under the amended Act](2026-06-23-parliament-atc-109-2026). Those memoranda are the mechanism by which the statistics office would obtain other departments' administrative data, which makes them the operative instrument rather than the Act.

Nothing states which departments they cover or when they are expected.

summary: The regulator issued a [precedent-setting access-to-information enforcement notice against a private body in June 2026](2026-06-16-paia-enforcement-mining-house-sibanye), the first of its kind on the record.
developments:
2026-06 — the Information Regulator [issued an enforcement notice against a mining company under the access-to-information Act](2026-06-16-paia-enforcement-mining-house-sibanye), which the account records as precedent-setting for private bodies. Before this window the base held no enforcement notice of any kind.

It is one notice, not a series. The regulator publishes no enforcement register, and the base holds no figure for requests made, refused or appealed under the Act, so what can be said is that the power was used and not how often it is needed.

summary: The regulator has [issued four enforcement notices since May](2026-08-31-itweb-inforeg-alarming-data-breaches), the latest to the national bureau of standards, and [took its school-results challenge to the Supreme Court of Appeal after three losses in the high court](2026-08-17-businessday-information-regulator-sca-matric-results-popia).
developments:
2026-05/06 — enforcement began. The regulator [issued its first enforcement notice for 2026 in May](2026-06-14-inforeg-first-enforcement-notice-2026), a [precedent-setting access-to-information notice against a mining company in June](2026-06-16-paia-enforcement-mining-house-sibanye), and a third treating a misdirected email as a reportable breach.

2026-08-31 — a fourth notice went to [the national bureau of standards over its 2024 ransomware attack, giving it 90 days to revise policies, run personal-information impact assessments and implement security measures](2026-08-31-itweb-inforeg-alarming-data-breaches), the regulator finding it had processed personal information unlawfully. Two direct-marketing matters were [referred to the enforcement committee under section 69, on unsolicited electronic communications](2026-08-31-itweb-inforeg-alarming-data-breaches), against more than 3,800 complaints in the previous year of which about a tenth concerned direct marketing.

2026-08-17 — it [lodged an appeal to the Supreme Court of Appeal over newspaper publication of school-leaving results](2026-08-17-businessday-information-regulator-sca-matric-results-popia), having lost three bids in the high court, arguing the education department must release results directly to learners and has no contract or legal basis for press publication.

Against that, it [stated on 18 August that it has no capability to test external systems for privacy compliance before launch](2026-08-18-timeslive-sahrc-personal-information-digital-age). The reporting rail it depends on has been in place since [the mandatory breach-reporting e-portal opened in April 2025](2025-04-15-mandatory-eportal-breach-reporting).

progress: Mixed, the regulator signalled enforcement while a nine-month credential exposure went unreported
summary: The regulator set out new enforcement signals ([briefing](2026-08-31-werksmans-popia-paia-enforcement-signals)) in a month when a nine-month credential exposure surfaced ([report](2026-09-01-itweb-hungry-lion-data-breach)).
developments:
The Information Regulator set out enforcement signals for data-protection and access-to-information compliance at a briefing on 31 August 2026 ([briefing](2026-08-31-werksmans-popia-paia-enforcement-signals)).

Stealer-log analysis found a fast-food chain's customer credentials exposed for about nine months through its web self-service portals, 13 of the 23 records being customer accounts ([report](2026-09-01-itweb-hungry-lion-data-breach)).

2026-08-31 — the regulator reported [more than 8,000 security-compromise reports to date and 1,220 since April, roughly 244 a month, projected to pass 3,000 for the year and called "very alarming"](2026-08-31-itweb-inforeg-alarming-data-breaches); its assessments [find the public sector putting less effort than the private into appropriate security measures](2026-08-31-itweb-inforeg-alarming-data-breaches).

2026-04-14 — quarterly figures [put breaches at roughly 263 a month in the first quarter of 2026 against about 284 a month over April to November 2025](2026-04-14-inforeg-788-breaches-q1). The rate has eased across all three periods held while the cumulative total has not.

Retention practice surfaced through litigation rather than supervision: an operator [told the Constitutional Court that it retains only six months of operational data at a time and that no record links a message to any corresponding return call](2026-08-25-please-call-me-vodacom-data-that-didnt-exist).

summary: Digitised border systems were [made a regional chairship priority on 17 August 2026](2026-08-18-sanews-sadc-borders-gateways-digital-systems), with progress to be measured in crossing times rather than agreements signed.
developments:
2026-08-17 — one-stop border posts and digitised border systems were [named a priority of the country's regional chairship](2026-08-18-sanews-sadc-borders-gateways-digital-systems), tied to a corridor trip monitoring system integrating transport, immigration and customs data, to online permitting and operator accreditation, to the electronic travel authorisation, and to a proposed regional tourism visa.

The framing is unusually concrete for a chairship priority — progress is to be measured in border-crossing times reduced rather than agreements signed — but the measure has no baseline. No crossing time, target or timetable is published, and the priority and the measure of progress are both the chair's own.

summary: South Africa is [recorded as a non-signatory to the Malabo Convention](2026-08-14-ssa-health-data-governance-literature-review) in an August 2026 review, which finds regional frameworks fragmented and cross-border harmonisation weak.
developments:
2026-08-14 — a peer-reviewed review of health-data governance across four countries [records only one of them as a Malabo Convention signatory, and South Africa as a non-signatory](2026-08-14-ssa-health-data-governance-literature-review). It finds all four frameworks fragmented, with weak cross-border transfer harmonisation and capacity gaps.

The position is a standing one restated, not a change: nothing in the window records a ratification step, a cabinet memorandum or a stated intention either way. What the review adds is that the absence is not peculiar to South Africa but is the regional norm, which is the more useful half of the finding.

summary: The [regional real-time settlement system added the kwanza on 27 July 2026](2026-07-28-sadc-rtgs-kwanza-official), its first currency beyond the rand since 2013.
developments:
2026-07-27 — the [Southern African regional real-time gross settlement system added the Angolan kwanza](2026-07-28-sadc-rtgs-kwanza-official). The system had settled in rand alone since 2013, so this is the first widening of the settlement currency in thirteen years.

What the base does not hold is what it is worth: no volume, value, participant count or corridor breakdown is published for the system before or after the addition, so the direction is clear and the size of the step is not.

summary: Five southern African customs administrations adopted a joint roadmap for customs-to-customs data exchange ([roadmap](2026-08-31-farmersreviewafrica-southern-african-customs-administrations-agree-roadmap-for-faster)).
developments:
The customs administrations of Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe adopted a joint roadmap and action plan for customs-to-customs data exchange at a three-day meeting in Pretoria on 24-26 August 2026, hosted by the South African Revenue Service ([roadmap](2026-08-31-farmersreviewafrica-southern-african-customs-administrations-agree-roadmap-for-faster)).

It supersedes the bilateral arrangement the base previously held as the only cross-border customs data link on the record.

A roadmap is not an exchange: the base holds no connection in service, no data-sharing instrument signed and no date by which the roadmap is to be delivered.

summary: The Minimum Interoperability Standards and the government-wide enterprise architecture [have an update dated September 2026](2026-07-31-sa-operation-vulindlela-q1-2026-progress-report) and nothing published against it.
developments:
The standing instruments are the Minimum Interoperability Standards and the government-wide enterprise architecture. The only thing the window records about them is a date: the quarterly reform report [carries an update due in September 2026](2026-07-31-sa-operation-vulindlela-q1-2026-progress-report).

Nothing is published, gazetted or consulted in the twelve months, and no conformance requirement, testing regime or department-level compliance figure appears anywhere on the ledger — which matters more than the slipped date, because a standard nobody tests against is a document rather than a standard.

summary: A Digital Public Services Standard [sets a national lifecycle and quality baseline](2025-08-04-digital-public-services-standard), and [biometric and cryptographic standards went out for revision](2026-04-17-sabs-standards-matters-gazette-54520).
developments:
2025-08-04 — [a Digital Public Services Standard was issued under a public service circular, setting a national lifecycle and quality baseline for digital public services covering accessibility, security, ethics, testing and quality assurance, deployment and retirement](2025-08-04-digital-public-services-standard). Nothing of the kind existed before it, and no compliance report, assessment or departmental adoption count has been published against it.

2026-04-17 — [the standards body put drafts out for comment on biometric performance testing, biometric information protection and cryptographic module testing, revising the biometric interface and identification-card standards and proposing one service-management standard for withdrawal](2026-04-17-sabs-standards-matters-gazette-54520).

The sequence is worth noting: the standards that would govern biometric quality are being revised while the biometric systems reported elsewhere in this document are already in service.

summary: The [2026 National Radio Frequency Plan re-bases the allocation table on the ITU Radio Regulations 2024](2026-07-24-national-radio-frequency-plan-2026-nrfp-26) and aligns to the continental and regional plans.
developments:
2026-07-24 — the [National Radio Frequency Plan 2026 was gazetted](2026-07-24-national-radio-frequency-plan-2026-nrfp-26), [approved by the minister on 2 July](2026-07-29-malatsi-approves-2026-national-radio-frequency-plan). It [re-bases the 8.3 kHz to 3,000 GHz allocation table on the ITU Radio Regulations 2024](2026-07-24-national-radio-frequency-plan-2026-nrfp-26), keeps the country in ITU Region 1 with national variations only under the treaty's own reservation article, and aligns to the African and Southern African allocation plans. This is standards adoption in its plainest form: the national table now says what the international one says.

2026-08-03 — a second, quieter adoption. The medicines regulator [invited clinical-trial sponsors to report serious adverse events through the World Health Organization monitoring centre's module](2026-08-03-pilot-project-for-electronic-reporting-of-serious-adverse-events-vigiflow-module), routing domestic trial safety data through internationally hosted infrastructure and taking its reporting standard rather than writing one. No pilot duration, participant target, data-residency statement or transition date to mandatory reporting is published.

summary: The rights commission [published a policy brief on information integrity](2026-08-19-south-africa-sahrc-information-integrity-doj-speech) and a provincial cluster [convened a responsible-AI programme](2026-08-19-citizen-activate-sa-ai-policy-summit) after the national policy was withdrawn.
developments:
2026-08-19 — the rights commission [launched a policy brief on information integrity and human rights](2026-08-19-south-africa-sahrc-information-integrity-doj-speech), grounded in the constitutional rights to expression, political participation and access to information, with a deputy minister stating that government should not become the custodian of truth on disinformation while the information environment should not be left to private platforms' algorithms. It is a brief rather than an instrument, and no legislative proposal or timetable follows from it on the record.

2026-08-17 — a provincial AI cluster [announced a responsible-AI programme with the provincial economic development department](2026-08-19-citizen-activate-sa-ai-policy-summit), holding its first summit on 25 August 2026 on policy, governance, infrastructure investment and sovereign AI. It was convened after the national department withdrew the draft national AI policy, so what is on the record is non-state and subnational actors filling a gap rather than feeding into a process.

summary: The electoral commission is [moving a disinformation code from draft to enforcement before the local elections](2026-08-24-citizen-iec-electoral-code-disinformation), binding contestants against campaigning on falsehoods.
developments:
2026-08-24 — the electoral commission [is moving its updated code of conduct on countering disinformation from draft to enforcement ahead of the local government elections](2026-08-24-citizen-iec-electoral-code-disinformation). The existing code is extended to campaign mechanisms on new, digital and social media, and binds political contestants, candidates and their supporters against campaigning on falsehoods, with disinformation defined as false information circulated in the knowledge that it is false.

The commission cannot itself find a breach or impose a sanction: where it investigates and forms the opinion that one may have occurred it must refer the matter to the Electoral Court. Alongside the code it is working with large platform companies on self-regulation, so that false content can be referred to them for takedown — which places a private takedown route beside a judicial one, with no published standard governing the first. [The draft was gazetted with a comment deadline the commission's own statement dates differently from the notice](2026-06-30-iec-draft-electoral-code-conduct-countering-disinformation), and it is a draft rather than promulgated regulations.

summary: The communications department [spent R3.61bn of a R3.74bn budget in 2025/26](2026-03-26-zaf-agsa-pfma-2024-25-government-ict-findings), a near-full draw and the only domestic financing figure the base holds.
developments:
The one domestic budget figure on the ledger is a [spend of R3.61bn against R3.74bn appropriated for 2025/26](2026-03-26-zaf-agsa-pfma-2024-25-government-ict-findings), a near-full draw with no prior year on file to compare it against.

What it cannot answer is whether the financing is sustainable, because the ledger holds no forward estimate, no capital and current split and no measure of what the money bought. The one place a shortfall is visible is elsewhere in this report: the flagship broadband programme's in-year allocation collapsed and the programme was closed rather than completed, which is a financing outcome that no departmental spend rate would have shown.

summary: Eleven institutions [were named as joint partners in the national data exchange pilot at its launch](2025-10-03-national-treasury-launches-mzansixchange-pilot-advisory), the only multi-party arrangement on this ledger.
developments:
2025-10-03 — [eleven institutions were named as joint partners in the national data exchange pilot at its launch](2025-10-03-national-treasury-launches-mzansixchange-pilot-advisory). Nothing comparable existed on this ledger before it.

No memorandum text, term or financial commitment is published for any of the eleven, so what is established is that the arrangement exists and who is in it, not what any party has undertaken to do.

It matters because the exchange it supports has no statute, reported under legislation: a set of institutional relationships is currently doing the work a legal framework would otherwise do.

summary: A fibre group was [recapitalised at a combined R8.4bn equity value](2026-08-24-frogfoot-fibre-rollout-capital-itweb) and a data-centre operator [holds a ZAR7.5bn expansion budget](2026-08-12-south-africa-equinix-joburg-data-centre-expansion) — neither disclosing money actually raised — while a [venture fund reached a R300m first close](2026-08-31-itweb-co-za-mamor-capital-r300m).
developments:
2026-08-24 — new shares were [subscribed across three fibre and telecoms companies at a combined after-debt equity value of R8.4bn](2026-08-24-frogfoot-fibre-rollout-capital-itweb), with the rollout stated to reach 360,000 connected homes a year within twelve months. The subscription amount is not disclosed: [the R8.4bn is the implied equity value of the companies, not the money raised](2026-08-24-frogfoot-fibre-rollout-capital-itweb), and the targets are the parties' own.

2026-08-12 — an international data-centre operator [reported scaling its Johannesburg facility to 24MW against a ZAR7.5bn South African expansion budget](2026-08-12-south-africa-equinix-joburg-data-centre-expansion) covering that site plus banked land in two cities, with further build-out held pending demand.

Both figures are the private parties' own, and neither is a commitment a reader can hold anyone to. Private capital is clearly the larger source of digital investment here than the state budget, and it is also the source the base can measure least well.

2026-08-31 — a black women-owned venture firm [reached a R300m first close against a R550m target, anchored by the state asset manager](2026-08-31-itweb-co-za-mamor-capital-r300m), to back post-revenue technology companies; its founder says [the raise took more than three years and that institutional appetite remains undeveloped](2026-08-31-mamor-capital-ventures-first-fund-close-south-africa). A first close is committed, not deployed, capital.

summary: A UK-funded regional science and technology accelerator [opened expressions of interest on 11 August 2026](2026-08-11-fcdo-sta-s-southern-africa-programme), worth up to GBP2.5m to March 2030 with South Africa its primary focus.
developments:
2026-08-11 — [expressions of interest opened for a Southern Africa science and technology accelerator](2026-08-11-fcdo-sta-s-southern-africa-programme), [up to GBP2.5m over three years to March 2030 with up to GBP400,000 for 2026/27](2026-08-11-uk-fcdo-xsa-2026-sta-s), covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and digital access alongside climate, energy, health and space. South Africa is the primary focus and two neighbouring countries the first year's.

It is at expressions-of-interest stage: the fund is resourced but the delivery consortium is not chosen, and contract signature is expected within 2026. The programme therefore has a ceiling and a subject matter and nothing else yet, and it arrived in the final fortnight of this window — so what is reported is an arrival, not twelve months of movement.

summary: 93.8% of households held a cellphone only in 2025, with 3.7% having no telephone at all ([figures](2026-08-28-mobile-penetration-groundup)).
developments:
Official household figures charted and published in August 2026 record 93.8% of households holding a cellphone only in 2025, 2.5% holding both a cellphone and a landline, and 3.7% — about 740,000 households — holding no telephone at all, against nearly 55% with none in 2002 ([figures](2026-08-28-mobile-penetration-groundup)).

The only subscription movement the base holds for the window is at the resale layer. An analyst house [put active virtual-operator SIMs at about 4.4 million at end-2025, up roughly 43% year on year and forecast to reach 14.4 million by 2030](2026-08-20-itweb-mvno-market-south-africa), placing the country first on the continent. One operator separately [reported 5.7 million virtual-operator subscribers on its own wholesale platform for the twelve months to 31 May 2026](2026-08-21-cell-c-gains-1-3m-subscribers-reduces-debt), which it put at an estimated 80 to 85% share.

The two are not a series and cannot be netted: one counts SIMs across the market on an undisclosed method, the other counts subscribers on a single platform. No regulator return and no operator-reported national subscriber figure appears on this ledger, so growth in resale is visible and total penetration is not.

summary: The regulator [puts household internet access at 82.1% and fixed internet at home at 17.4%](2026-03-31-icasa-state-of-the-ict-sector-report-2026), with fourth-generation coverage at 99.5%.
developments:
2026-03-31 — the sector report [puts fourth-generation population coverage at 99.5% and fifth-generation at 58.0%, household internet access at 82.1% and fixed internet at home at 17.4%, with 4,377 of 21,878 government facilities connected as at October 2025](2026-03-31-icasa-state-of-the-ict-sector-report-2026), against [the prior year's edition](2025-03-31-icasa-state-of-the-ict-sector-report-2025).

Two of those figures are the finding. The gap between household access and fixed access at home says almost all use is mobile, which sets what a household can do with it. And a fifth of government facilities connected, in a country with near-universal mobile coverage, locates the problem in the state's own estate rather than in the network.

It is the only regulator-published usage series on this ledger.

progress: Mixed, a data-rollover regulation gazetted and under legal challenge while device prices rose against an excise cut
summary: Unused bundles [must roll over from January 2027](2026-01-23-icasa-end-user-and-subscriber-service-charter-amendment-regulations), a rule [now under review application by two operators](2026-07-30-malatsi-data-expiry-regulation-south-africa); an excise cut is [offset by rising device prices](2026-08-20-ai-driving-up-africa-smartphone-prices).
developments:
2026-01-23 — amendment regulations were [gazetted requiring unused data bundles to roll over automatically and free of charge at least once](2026-01-23-icasa-end-user-and-subscriber-service-charter-amendment-regulations), excluding bundles of seven days or less and uncapped, free and promotional bundles, with depletion alerts at 50%, 80% and 100%. They come into force on 23 January 2027. [Two operators have filed for review](2026-07-30-malatsi-data-expiry-regulation-south-africa), and the filing date and case number are unestablished.

On devices the two forces run opposite ways. The minister [credits the April 2025 excise removal with 1.1m additional entry-level units](2026-07-10 SOLLY MALATSI  Removing smartphone tax means access to opportunity); against that, [African sub-$100 smartphone shipments fell 34% year on year in the second quarter of 2026 and the continental average selling price rose $41 to $202](2026-08-20-ai-driving-up-africa-smartphone-prices), attributed to memory and semiconductor demand. A tax cut and a component-cost rise are working on the same price, and the base holds no South-Africa-specific unit or price series to net them against.

progress: Mixed, a programme closed and a merger deferred while a rapid-deployment Bill and a wholesale network moved
summary: The flagship broadband programme was [declared ended](2026-02-25-zaf-itweb-budget-2026-sa-connect-phase-two-ends) and the state network merger [pushed to FY2028/29](2026-04-28 State broadband merger limps into a second decade), while an [amendment Bill on rapid deployment was tabled](2026-04-20-sa-electronic-communications-amendment-bill-b12-2026) and a [private wholesale 5G network opened](2026-08-20-techcentral-south-africa-comsol-5g-woan).
developments:
2026-02 — the flagship broadband programme [was declared ended in the Budget Review rather than completed](2026-02-25-zaf-itweb-budget-2026-sa-connect-phase-two-ends), against a 2022 cabinet target of universal access in 36 months.

2026-04-28 — the state network merger went backwards: the deliverable for the year was a finalised road map, and [the plan tabled in March 2026 starts again with a preliminary report and implementation in FY2028/29](2026-04-28 State broadband merger limps into a second decade).

2026-04-20 — an [Electronic Communications Amendment Bill was tabled](2026-04-20-sa-electronic-communications-amendment-bill-b12-2026) that would make not-for-profit network services licence-exempt and require a national standard by-law providing a uniform wayleave process; [the committee extended written submissions to 21 September 2026](2026-08-21-citizen-electronic-communications-bill-input-deadline). The regulator separately [moved to compel every licensed operator to submit geo-referenced data on all passive infrastructure twice a year](2026-04-12 Icasa moves to mandate national infrastructure database), with fines up to R1m.

2026-08 — a [privately financed wholesale 5G home-broadband network opened wholesale sales](2026-08-20-techcentral-south-africa-comsol-5g-woan), with the first retail provider due live in September 2026; its chief executive accepted the description that this is the open-access network the state spent a decade trying to licence. No coverage footprint, site count or wholesale price is published, so what entered service cannot be sized.

summary: A new subsea route [opened for business in December 2025 with two South African landings](2025-12-04-bayobab-2africa-west-open-for-business).
developments:
2025-12-04 — [the 2Africa West route opened for business with landings at Yzerfontein and Duynefontein](2025-12-04-bayobab-2africa-west-open-for-business), an in-window addition to international capacity where none had been recorded.

No capacity, price or utilisation figure is published for either landing, so the base can state that capacity was added and nothing about how much, at what cost, or to whom it is sold.

That is the standing weakness of this indicator for the country: cable landings are announced and the wholesale market they feed is not measured anywhere on this ledger.

summary: The Cape Town exchange [went live at two further data-centre sites in August 2026](2026-08-11-cinx-oadc-cape-town-expansion), reaching six locations while one facility still holds most of its peering.
developments:
2026-08-03 — the Cape Town internet exchange [went live at two further data-centre sites, taking it to six locations](2026-08-11-cinx-oadc-cape-town-expansion). More sites is the movement; concentration is what the same record shows underneath it. [One facility holds 87 of the exchange's 122 networks and nearly every 100 Gbps port, against 208 networks and 10,132 Gbps on the more distributed Johannesburg exchange](2026-08-11-cinx-oadc-cape-town-expansion).

Distribution across sites is not the same thing as resilience while a single building carries most of the peering, and the base holds no traffic, outage or failover figure for either exchange to test it against.

progress: Mixed, the licensing framework went backwards while a distribution route opened and fee rules were consulted
summary: The ministerial policy direction was [rejected by the regulator](2026-05-14-starlink-legal-deadend-icasa-rejects-bee) and the 30% equity requirement stands, while [a distributor deal took the route the Act already allows](2026-07-15-herotel-amazon-leo-distributor).
developments:
An instrument was issued and neutralised inside five months. A policy direction gazetted on 12 December 2025 to unblock satellite licensing was [rejected in May 2026](2026-05-14-starlink-legal-deadend-icasa-rejects-bee), and the 30% historically-disadvantaged equity requirement stands. The minister [publicly backs entry while conceding licensing is the regulator's alone](2026-08-20-itweb-malatsi-leo-icasa), and at the spectrum hearings the largest prospective entrant [pressed the regulator on how that requirement applies to the new gateway and user-terminal licence categories](2026-08-24-south-africa-icasa-spacex-spectrum-licensing-hearing) — which the draft does not say.

2026-07-15 — the market entered anyway by another door: [a satellite operator appointed a domestic distributor](2026-07-15-herotel-amazon-leo-distributor), the acquisition route the Act already permits, while [the other large constellation launched in its 27th African country without entering South Africa](2026-07-17-starlink-launches-27th-african-country-ivory-coast).

2026-05/08 — the fee rules moved. [Draft amendments to the spectrum and fees regulations were gazetted, with oral hearings on 19 and 20 August 2026](2026-08-07-icasa-public-hearings-draft-radio-frequency-spectrum-regulations) covering satellite registration, blanket licensing for terminal networks and protection of radio astronomy; the prospective entrant's [representations ask for flat per-licence fees and a ten-year minimum term](2026-06-29-spacex-icasa-spectrum-fees-representations).

summary: Delivered load moved from [about 350MW to about 390MW](2026-07-22-sa-data-centre-gold-rush-resource-crunch), with [one 50MW facility](2025-11-10-teraco-ct2-50mw-cape-town) the only completed build of scale in the window.
developments:
2026-07-22 — delivered live load [moved from roughly 350MW to roughly 390MW](2026-07-22-sa-data-centre-gold-rush-resource-crunch). Announced pipeline over the same period would take the national figure several times higher, so the gap between announced and delivered capacity is the finding rather than the increment.

2025-11 — the only completed facility of scale was a [Cape Town expansion adding 32MW to reach 50MW](2025-11-10-teraco-ct2-50mw-cape-town). 2026-07-14 — a second operator [cleared a municipal planning tribunal for a Cape Town site](2026-07-16-cape-town-tribunal-data-centre-greenlight), which is an approval and not capacity.

What the base does not hold is a national register: no regulator or department publishes site counts, capacity, utilisation or grid connections, so every figure here is an operator's or an analyst's.

2024-01-31 - a foreign hyperscaler declared its first African cloud region operational at Johannesburg, a year after picking the city, letting customers deploy from a domestic location ([cloud region](2024-01-31-googles-first-africa-cloud-region-now-operational)). No capacity, customer count or investment figure accompanies it.

2026-08-27 - a metropolitan council approved a developer's request to connect a proposed hyperscale campus at a special economic zone directly to the national utility rather than the municipal grid, for up to 556 MW, against a R3bn municipal and community infrastructure investment offered by the developer and objections from councillors ([campus](2026-08-29-southafrica-vexa-coega-ai-data-hub-power)).

The connection is what was approved; the campus has no capacity in service, construction start or completion date on file. A single requested connection of 556 MW set against national delivered load of roughly 390 MW is the measure of what the pipeline would ask of the grid.

summary: A domestically headquartered operator [acquired seven facilities from a foreign one, taking its capacity above 25 MW](2026-02-11-oadc-acquires-seven-ntt-data-centres-south-africa).
developments:
2025-12-31 — [an African operator completed its acquisition of seven facilities from a foreign operator after competition approval, taking its total capacity above 25 MW](2026-02-11-oadc-acquires-seven-ntt-data-centres-south-africa).

It is the one movement on this ledger in which national providers gain estate rather than international ones, and it is a transfer of existing capacity rather than new build — the megawatts changed owner, not the country's total.

No per-site capacity, tenancy or price figure is published. The country's larger data-centre story is reported under all providers, where the expansion is foreign-financed and under rights-commission inquiry.

progress: Advanced, on a procurement notice rather than a capability
summary: A development bank [invited a five-year managed disaster-recovery service](2026-01-31-dbsa-rfp004-2026-managed-draas), and a second institution [put out a server and storage upgrade](2025-03-10-idc-rfp-upgrade-it-server-and-storage-infrastructure).
developments:
2026-01-31 — [a five-year managed service was invited for backup, restore, disaster recovery, replication and business continuity](2026-01-31-dbsa-rfp004-2026-managed-draas), and 2025-03-10 — [a second development finance institution invited proposals to upgrade its server and storage infrastructure](2025-03-10-idc-rfp-upgrade-it-server-and-storage-infrastructure).

Both are procurement notices. They establish an intention to buy resilience rather than a capability in service, and neither has an award, value or completion on file.

That is the whole of the country's off-site backup record. No government-wide backup standard, no recovery-time objective and no continuity test appears anywhere on this ledger — against a state that lost a statistical series for five years to a cyber incident, reported under administrative statistics.

summary: The rights commission [opened submissions on whether data-centre frameworks meet constitutional obligations](2026-05-22-sahrc-call-for-submissions-data-centres-human-rights), on eleven themes including electricity demand, water use and cooling; submissions closed 30 July 2026.
developments:
2026-05-22 — the national human rights commission [called for written submissions](2026-05-22-sahrc-call-for-submissions-data-centres-human-rights) under its constitutional and statutory powers, to assess whether the legal, regulatory, environmental, governance and industry frameworks around data-centre development meet constitutional obligations and international human rights standards. The eleven themes include electricity demand and tariffs, water use and cooling, environmental and climate impact, electronic waste, land use and community participation.

2026-07-24 — a [civil-society organisation announced its submission](2026-07-24-acbio-submission-sahrc-data-centres-human-rights), which is held as an announcement only: the host serves the document itself to an automated fetch with a refusal and no archive copy exists.

2026-08-22 — the [commission's scrutiny was reported as running](2026-08-22-businessday-sahrc-data-centre-inquiry-hidden-cost-ai), with environmental groups warning that the infrastructure required to power the state's artificial-intelligence ambitions carries costs that have not been accounted for. No terms of reference, hearing date or reporting deadline is published, so an inquiry is open and its shape is not on the record.

summary: The energy availability factor [reached 67.55%, its highest in six years, with unplanned outages down 44.5%](2026-08-14-eskom-eaf-67-55-eastern-cape-load-reduction-free-aug-2026), against [a 2029-30 adequacy risk identified by the system operator](2025-10-30-ntcsa-medium-term-system-adequacy-outlook-2026-2030).
developments:
2026-08-14 — [the energy availability factor reached 67.55%, its highest in six years, with unplanned outages down 44.5% year on year, about 1.2 million customers removed from load reduction and 505,607 smart meters installed](2026-08-14-eskom-eaf-67-55-eastern-cape-load-reduction-free-aug-2026). 2025-09-29 — [the last unit of the two flagship build programmes entered commercial operation, adding 800 MW](2025-09-29-eskom-kusile-unit-6-commercial-operation).

Against the recovery, 2025-10-30 — [the system operator completed its medium-term adequacy assessment on a new multi-nodal, transmission-constrained method and identified a 2029-30 adequacy risk against an unserved-energy metric below 20 GWh](2025-10-30-ntcsa-medium-term-system-adequacy-outlook-2026-2030).

The method change is the substantive part: adequacy is now assessed against the transmission network rather than generation alone, which is the constraint the data-centre load reported elsewhere on this ledger runs into.

summary: The electrification grant [spent 17.6% by the third quarter with over R190 million unspent](2026-05-12-zaf-parliament-unrevised-hansard-12-may-2026), against [1.6 million households still unelectrified](2025-10-30-zaf-parliament-committee-electrify-16-million-households-2030).
developments:
2025-10-30 — [household electrification stood at 94.7% with 1.6 million households still unelectrified, about three million without metered supply once illegal connections are counted, against a grant allocation of R3.9 billion for 2025/26 including R247 million for solar home systems](2025-10-30-zaf-parliament-committee-electrify-16-million-households-2030).

2026-05-12 — [roughly R4 billion for 2026/27 was set against third-quarter spending of 17.6% and under-expenditure of more than R190 million, attributed to late service-provider appointments and municipal non-compliance](2026-05-12-zaf-parliament-unrevised-hansard-12-may-2026).

2025-07-11 — [the grant is being repurposed toward universal access through micro-grid and off-grid solutions](2025-07-11-zaf-ramokgopa-electricity-energy-budget-vote-2025-26), with more than 1.6 million households, many of them rural, in energy poverty.

Money allocated and not spent, against a stated target year of 2030, is what makes this stalled rather than slow.

progress: Mixed, front-office downtime fell sharply while the national computing pillar hit its ceiling
summary: Home Affairs downtime [fell 61% to 13,867 hours in 2025/26](2026-08-11-south-africa-pmg-home-affairs-downtime-question-nw2745), while the national high-performance computing centre is [reported at maximum capacity](2026-08-05-sa-parliament-committee-nicis-oversight-visit).
developments:
2026-08-11 — a parliamentary reply [put nationwide system downtime at 13,867 hours in 2025/26 against 35,426 the year before, a 61% reduction](2026-08-11-south-africa-pmg-home-affairs-downtime-question-nw2745), with provincial gains ranging from 79% to 41%, attributed to a service-level upgrade at the state IT agency, 226 links migrated to fibre and 439 offices running on the identification system. The reply is the fuller record: the population register's own downtime [fell only from 14,720 to 11,479 hours, a 22% improvement](2026-08-10-south-africa-home-affairs-downtime-official-statement), which is not the figure the department led with.

2026-08-05 — the other direction. A committee oversight visit [reported the national high-performance computing centre at maximum capacity and available infrastructure insufficient for future growth](2026-08-05-sa-parliament-committee-nicis-oversight-visit).

2026-08-24 — and the estate below both: a [fifteen-year tender for inmate communications across 243 correctional centres](2026-08-24-sa-top-ict-tenders-inmate-telephone-system-itweb) states the existing copper telephony has deteriorated beyond support. No contract value is published and nothing is awarded.

summary: An investigation into the state IT agency [reported R2.07bn of irregular expenditure across four audited years](2026-07-06-sita-r2bn-irregular-spending) and annual performance achievement of 42.86%.
developments:
2026-07 — a public service commission investigation into the state IT agency [reported R2.07bn of irregular expenditure across four audited years and governance weaknesses](2026-07-06-sita-r2bn-irregular-spending), with annual performance plan achievement of 42.86% in 2024/25. The agency is [separately described as slowing government technology rollout](2026-07-07 South Africa's state IT agency is slowing government tech rollout).

The 30-day deadline for a recovery plan expired inside this window and no plan is on the record. The agency is the shared capability every department's systems depend on, so a finding of this size against it is a statement about the state's ability to build and run its own systems rather than about one entity's audit outcome.

progress: Mixed, a breach at the national computing centre and no re-measurement, against a remediation programme and a training tender
summary: The national supercomputer was [breached and remediated](2026-08-19-rsa-na-written-reply-nw4186-chpc-lengau-cyber-security-incident), the [national CSIRT publishes no incident statistics](2026-08-04-cybersecurity-hub-south-africa-national-csirt-incident-management-and-reporting), and [no national measurement was repeated](2024-10-31-csir-national-cybersecurity-survey-2024-data-breaches) in the window.
developments:
2026-05 — the national high-performance computing centre suffered [unauthorised access and the deployment of crypto-mining malware](2026-08-19-rsa-na-written-reply-nw4186-chpc-lengau-cyber-security-incident), attributed in an August written reply to vulnerabilities in the legacy system, with ageing components no longer fully supported by their vendors. A [remediation and resilience programme has since run across access controls, privileged-access management, network segmentation, patch management and monitoring](2026-08-24-lengau-supercomputer-breach-cause-chpc-itweb), with an internal accountability review still running. No cost, data-loss finding or outage duration is stated and the account is the department's own.

2026-08-04 — the [national CSIRT is operating, coordinating and routing reports rather than resolving them, on weekdays from 08:00 to 16:30 with no published out-of-hours capability](2026-08-04-cybersecurity-hub-south-africa-national-csirt-incident-management-and-reporting). As at that date it published no incident statistics, advisories archive, annual report or data downloads.

The national measurement has not been repeated: the [2024 surveys remain the last](2024-10-31-csir-national-cybersecurity-survey-2024-data-breaches), on breaches and on the [skills gap](2024-10-31-csir-national-cybersecurity-survey-2024-skills-gap). One firm's caseload [put ransomware dwell time at 18 days in 2025 against 117 in 2024](2026-08-11-sa-ransomware-dwell-time-cyanre) — faster attack execution rather than improved defence, and not a national series.

summary: The pilot [has infrastructure operational at the national research council with four departments testing it](2026-01-01-operation-vulindlela-phase-ii-progress-report-q3-2025-26), on a term [ending in September 2026](2026-06-23-parliament-atc-109-2026).
developments:
2025-10-09 — [a one-year pilot launched](2025-10-10-mzansixchange-launch), built on the Estonian data-exchange design: [a federated real-time sharing rail rather than a central repository](2025-11-05-govt-data-exchange-estonia-xroad), with [four task teams, interoperability standards and draft data-exchange legislation as its deliverables](2025-09-27-mzansixchange-pilot-programme).

2026-01 — [pilot infrastructure is operational at the national research council, with home affairs, the social security agency, the student aid scheme and the public service department testing it and a working single-citizen application prototype built](2026-01-01-operation-vulindlela-phase-ii-progress-report-q3-2025-26). That answers the participating-department question this row previously could not.

2026-07 — [nine months in, it was onboarding additional technical capacity to support completion](2026-07-31-sa-operation-vulindlela-q1-2026-progress-report), and [the pilot ends in September 2026](2026-06-23-parliament-atc-109-2026). No volume of records exchanged is published, and no source states what decision the pilot's end triggers or who takes it.

summary: Biometric verification of grant recipients against the population register reached [997,379 of 19.05m recipients by March 2026](2026-05-18-parliamentary-question-nw1941-sassa-biometric-verification), about five per cent.
developments:
Compulsory for new applications from September 2025, biometric verification against the home affairs register [had reached 997,379 of 19.05m recipients by March 2026](2026-05-18-parliamentary-question-nw1941-sassa-biometric-verification), against 42,000 in its first two weeks.

That is about five per cent of the recipient base after seven months, so the mechanism works and the coverage does not yet mean much. It is also the clearest instance on this ledger of one state system drawing on another's identity data across a whole population, and the base holds no statement of the legal basis, the error rate or what happens to a recipient the check fails.

summary: The health interoperability architecture [remains the gazetted 2021 normative standards framework](2022-10-21-south-africa-hnsf-2021-interoperability-digital-health-gazette), with no implementation measurement held and the Act it underpins before the Constitutional Court.
developments:
The architecture is defined inside a [gazetted 2021 normative standards framework for interoperability in digital health](2022-10-21-south-africa-hnsf-2021-interoperability-digital-health-gazette) rather than in a document of its own: a federated hybrid of local and shared infrastructure, with central patient, provider and facility registries, shared clinical repositories and a national health information exchange, built on the international profile and messaging standards. It superseded the 2014 framework and states that semantic interoperability remains an ongoing undertaking with value sets to be published in due time.

Nothing in the window measures what it delivered. [The insurance scheme it underpins is in its second phase to 2028, its Act is under constitutional challenge with judgment reserved since May, and the national patient registration system is still being built](2026-08-20-itweb-nhi-telemedicine).

progress: Mixed, the school administration system entered user testing while the post-school learner platform was put at risk by an ownership dispute
summary: School administration modernisation [entered user acceptance testing](2026-02-04-dbe-sa-sams-modernisation-uat), while the post-school learner platform [is at risk from an intellectual-property dispute](2026-08-20-parliament-ilms-intellectual-property-dispute).
developments:
2026-02-04 — [user acceptance testing began on the modernised school administration system ahead of phased national implementation, with provincial education information officials and the state IT agency participating](2026-02-04-dbe-sa-sams-modernisation-uat). The standing interoperability instrument beneath it is [an education data-coding standard of 2011](2011-06-06-sc009-standard-for-data-coding), which has not been revised on the record.

2026-08-20 — against that, [an intellectual-property dispute and weak departmental buy-in put the post-school integrated learner management system at risk, with the shared platform piloting in sector education authorities](2026-08-20-parliament-ilms-intellectual-property-dispute).

The dispute is over who owns the platform rather than what it does, which is the failure mode a shared system in the public sector is most exposed to and the one least visible in a delivery report.

progress: Advanced, an integration plan ordered rather than built
summary: The Public Protector [found the student funding scheme insufficiently integrated with home affairs, social security and revenue data, and gave the board 30 days to produce a plan](2026-08-19-itweb-nsfas-30-days-ict-modernisation).
developments:
2026-08-18 — the Public Protector [found the student funding scheme's systems insufficiently integrated with the home affairs, social security and revenue data sources it needs to verify students](2026-08-19-itweb-nsfas-30-days-ict-modernisation), and directed a digital modernisation and systems-integration plan within 30 days covering institutional integration, verification interfaces, fraud controls and cyber security, elimination of duplicate applications and manual workarounds, student-facing case tracking and costed milestones.

[The report draws on a 2023 investigation that found some 40,000 non-qualifying students funded to more than R5.1bn, and records that the scheme cannot resolve 80% of contact-centre queries without internal escalation](2026-08-19-itweb-nsfas-30-days-ict-modernisation). What has advanced is an order with a deadline attached; no plan, integration or interface is on the record.

summary: Every stated date moved: [hosting is now 31 March 2027 and credentials 2027/28](2026-04-21 South Africa's digital ID gets a targeted launch date), and the [digital driving licence's nearest milestone is March 2027](2026-01-07 Digital driving licence coming to South Africa).
developments:
The schedule slipped at every stated milestone. A deadline of April 2025 for cabinet approval of the legal framework was missed; the roadmap milestone of a functional digital identity by the end of the 2025 financial year was missed; the President told Parliament in February 2026 that digital identity would launch during 2026; and the department's own plan, tabled six weeks later, [put hosting at 31 March 2027 and operation at 2027/28](2026-04-21 South Africa's digital ID gets a targeted launch date).

[The plan's only target for 2026/27 is the hosting infrastructure itself](2026-03-30-dha-annual-performance-plan-2026-27-digital-identity), with verifiable credentials via a digital wallet in 2027/28 and digital identity and e-passports by 2029. [Core identity and PKI infrastructure is to be hosted within the revenue service's environment](2026-05-20-home-affairs-828m-digital-id-budget), with the central bank integrating on payments and know-your-customer checks, and facial recognition primary with fingerprints secondary.

The digital driving licence moved the same way: [promised for 2026, its nearest dated milestone is now March 2027](2026-01-07 Digital driving licence coming to South Africa).

About 300,000 identity documents are blocked behind court orders where duplicates or people illegally in the country were detected, and the minister puts the great majority of identity-theft cases on the manual green identity book, still held by about 16 million people ([minister](2026-08-27-timeslive-home-affairs-id-fraud-smart-id)).

summary: Smart identity services ran at [410 bank branches by 13 August 2026, with 574,371 applications processed through banks](2026-08-21-businessday-home-affairs-750-bank-branches-smart-id), against 30 branches a year earlier.
developments:
2026-08-21 — a departmental reply to Parliament [put 410 bank branches live as at 13 August 2026 and 574,371 applications processed through banks](2026-08-21-businessday-home-affairs-750-bank-branches-smart-id), against 30 branches across five banks in August 2025. The department commits to at least 200 more and states a possibility of 750 branches during 2026/27, and separately to modernising 75 of the 145 remaining unmodernised local offices this financial year. A [public branch locator is published](2026-08-05-dha-smart-id-bank-branch-locator).

2026-01-28 — issuance itself set a record: [4,002,964 smart identity documents in 2025, up 17%](2026-01-28 Home Affairs sets new record by delivering over four million Smart IDs in 2025).

The branch counts do not form a series — 372 and 408 appear a week apart in August before the 410 in the reply — and the 750 is a possibility stated to Parliament rather than a target. This is the largest measurable delivery in the twelve months, and it is a channel expansion rather than a new system.

summary: Third-party use of the population register [was priced from July 2025 at R10 a verification, with the revenue earmarked for the system's maintenance](2025-06-23-identification-regulations-fourteenth-amendment-gazette-52893).
developments:
2025-06-23 — [a price was gazetted for third-party use of the population register: R10 per real-time verification and R1 per batch field, free to state departments, municipalities and statutory bodies, in force 1 July 2025](2025-06-23-identification-regulations-fourteenth-amendment-gazette-52893), [the department describing it as correcting unsustainable under-pricing of a service it has run since 2013 and earmarking the revenue for the system's maintenance](2025-06-23-dha-npr-verification-service-pricing-correction).

That is the only funded maintenance arrangement for an identity system on this ledger, and it is unusual in kind: the system is maintained out of what banks and other private verifiers pay to query it.

No maintenance spend, uptime figure or upgrade programme is published against that revenue.

summary: The [online verification service is running with its fee under review litigation](2025-07-06 Home Affairs on launch of world-class new identity verification service and cost), and no accuracy, volume or uptime measure for it is held.
developments:
The standing position is an [online identity verification service in operation, with its fee the subject of a review application](2025-07-06 Home Affairs on launch of world-class new identity verification service and cost). Nothing in the twelve months to 2026-08-26 resolves that litigation or changes the service.

What the base does not hold is any measure of it: no query volume, no match accuracy, no uptime and no list of which institutions consume it. The one adjacent movement is in the draft identification regulations, which would grant accredited trusted entities interface access to the population register under data-sharing agreements — a second authentication route, not yet made, and reported under the legislation indicator rather than here.

summary: 680,555 babies [were registered within 30 days of birth in 2025/26 against a 677,000 target](2026-05-15-dha-highest-ever-smart-id-output-2025-26), with automation in health facilities still planned.
developments:
2026-05-15 — [680,555 babies were registered within 30 days of birth in 2025/26 against a target of 677,000, with automation of the birth process in health facilities still planned for 2026/27](2026-05-15-dha-highest-ever-smart-id-output-2025-26). It is the department's own figure and no total-births denominator is given, so the share registered in time is not derivable.

The statutory basis is old and unchanged: [the Births and Deaths Registration Act has been in force since 1992](1992-05-06-births-and-deaths-registration-act-51-of-1992), held as an excerpt.

The link to a credential is what the white paper reported under interoperability proposes to build; today the registration is timely and the identity that follows from it is a separate transaction.

summary: Cabinet [approved a white paper anchoring digital identity in an intelligent population register with real-time integration and digitally enabled mandatory birth and death registration](2026-04-08-cabinet-approves-revised-white-paper-citizenship).
developments:
2026-04-08 — [Cabinet approved the Revised White Paper on Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection, anchoring civil-registration reform in turning the National Population Register into an Intelligent Population Register through biometrics, interoperability and real-time integration as the foundation for digital identity, alongside digitally enabled mandatory birth and death registration](2026-04-08-cabinet-approves-revised-white-paper-citizenship).

It is a white paper rather than a bill, and the identification statute it anticipates is carried separately on this ledger.

What it states plainly is the design: registration at birth and the digital credential are to be one system rather than two, which is the position this indicator asks about and which no instrument has yet delivered. No timetable, cost or architecture is published with it.

summary: Home affairs [built the Treasury a real-time biometric employee-verification portal against the population register](2026-05-26-dha-treasury-employee-verification-platform), with go-live stated for June 2026.
developments:
2026-05-26 — [a real-time biometric employee-verification portal was built for the National Treasury and linked to the population register, to detect payroll records with no matching person, with go-live stated as 15 June 2026](2026-05-26-dha-treasury-employee-verification-platform).

No confirmation that go-live occurred, and no count of records checked or discrepancies found, is on file.

It is the clearest case on this ledger of the identity layer being consumed by another department's system rather than by a bank, and it is priced: the verification service it runs on charges per query, reported under national maintenance. A payroll integrity check that costs the state money per employee is a design choice nothing on the record discusses.

summary: The central bank [ruled out non-bank shareholding in the payments utility it half-owns](2026-08-01-no-plans-to-add-non-banks-to-payinc-shareholding-kganyago) and [restated that a retail digital currency has no compelling case](2026-07-02-sarb-payments-first-over-cbdc).
developments:
2026-07-31 — the Governor told the Bank's ordinary general meeting that it [would have preferred to hold all of the payments utility and is not looking at bringing others in](2026-08-01-no-plans-to-add-non-banks-to-payinc-shareholding-kganyago), having acquired 50% in October 2025. The installed base around it was put at 39 participating banks and more than 480 non-bank payment service providers.

2026-06 — on digital currency the position hardened rather than moved: the Bank's published view is that [a retail central bank digital currency has no compelling case yet and the everyday rails come first](2026-07-02-sarb-payments-first-over-cbdc), with its wholesale distributed-ledger work confined to two completed projects.

Both are the same posture from two directions — the central bank taking ownership of the shared retail rail while declining to issue a retail instrument of its own.
